prime.problem: Eleven cards of fixes are easy to finish as eleven separate tricks: shrink W2, shrink W1, use 5/3, add BatchNorm, plot things. Without the causal map that joins them, you can retype the code but can't say which fix to reach for when a new net won't train, or why BatchNorm makes some of the earlier fixes unnecessary and not others.
prime.fits: This is the front page of course 5, read first as the map or last as the recap. It takes the z2h-4 MLP as it is (same data, same loop, dev loss about 2.17) and asks why it starts so badly. It leans on micrograd's tanh backward (1 − t²) and the toolkit's "variances add". The next course writes every one of these layers' backward passes by hand, BatchNorm included.
expect: BatchNorm: batch statistics, γ and β, running buffers
per-layer histograms and the update:data ratio ≈ −3
prime.goal: Draw the whole course as one causal map, from a random init to a deep stack you can see into, and for each lever (output scale, hidden scale, gain, BN, momentum, lr) say what it changes and the number it produced.

attend: The starter net has two separate scale problems at step 0. Which one does the step-0 loss reveal, and which one is invisible to it?
Three fixes set the hidden layer's scale: W1 × 0.2, gain / √fan_in, BatchNorm. What does each one depend on, and what does each one stop depending on?
BatchNorm makes the activations indifferent to the gain. Which quantity is still not indifferent, and which plot is the only one that shows it?
Where in the course does the batch start to matter for a single example's output, and what three things (a buffer, a flag, a bias) exist only because of it?
On the one-layer MLP, BN gives val 2.1057 against Kaiming's 2.1070. What does the lecture use instead to argue that BN is worth it?

must: Every unit sums fan_in random terms → with std-1 weights the spread grows by √fan_in per layer → logits of std 12.75 make softmax confidently wrong (27.8817 vs ln 27 = 3.2958) and hpreact of std 5.18 parks 61% of tanh outputs in their flat tails → shrink the output layer (W2 × 0.01, b2 × 0) and scale the hidden one by gain / √fan_in ((5/3)/√30 = 0.3043)

tanh's backward multiplies by 1 − t² → near ±1 it passes almost nothing (0.0199 at t = 0.99) → saturated units learn slowly and a unit flat on every example is dead → in a deep stack these gates compound → per-layer histograms must show similar std and few saturated units at every depth (gain 5/3: std ≈ 0.66, about 5%)

Init only sets step 0 and depth multiplies any error → BatchNorm standardises each unit over the batch on every forward pass, then γ and β give the freedom back → activations sit at std 0.63–0.65 whatever the gain, and a bias before BN is subtracted away (grad 4.4e-10) → bias=False, the ResNet motif

BN's statistics come from the batch → an example's output depends on its batchmates (2.2× swing) and a batch of 1 gives nan → running buffers (EMA, momentum 0.001), updated without gradients and used in eval mode (val 2.1057 vs calibrated 2.1056) → but BN divides out the weight scale, so the gradient scales by 1/c and the update:data ratio by 1/c² → the lr still has to be tuned, read off ud ≈ −3
elevated: Layers written as classes with one contract (__call__, .parameters(), .out, .training) → the net is a list and every probe is a loop over it → a 6-layer, 47,024-parameter stack is as easy to inspect as the one-layer MLP, and the .training flag is where the BN test-time bug lives
reference: the chapter timestamps and the loss log (2.1682 → 2.13 → 2.1027 → 2.1070 → 2.1048 in the notebook; the labs measure 2.1698, 2.1311, 2.1027, 2.1070, 2.1057)
thresholds: |h| > 0.99 for the saturation picture, |t| > 0.97 in the histogram printout

compress.prompt: Course-level compress: without looking, draw the whole course's causal map on one page. Start from "weights drawn from randn" and end at "a deep stack that trains, and you can prove it". Put the eleven cards as boxes in the order they are needed, draw an arrow for each because, and mark the three places where the loss alone would not have told you anything was wrong.
checklist: randn weights → spread grows √fan_in → confidently wrong logits (seen in the step-0 loss) and saturated tanh (not seen in the loss)
fix by hand (W2 × 0.01, W1 × 0.2) → by rule (gain / √fan_in) → automatically every step (BatchNorm with γ, β)
the gate 1 − t² and flat regions explain why saturation and dead ReLUs stop learning
BN couples the batch → running buffers, the training flag, bias=False
layer classes with .out → histograms per layer, then update:data for the step size
invisible to the loss: saturated hidden units, a wrong per-layer gain, a step size off by 25× under BN

retrieve.q: Explain to a programmer who knows the z2h-4 MLP why its step-0 loss is 27.88 and not 3.30, and why fixing that alone still leaves the net half broken.
answer: a model that knows nothing should give every character 1/27, a loss of ln 27 = 3.2958
each logit sums 200 h·W2 terms with std-1 weights, std ≈ 13, so softmax bets hard on arbitrary characters: confidently wrong
W2 × 0.01, b2 × 0 gives 3.3221, but W1 is still std-1, so hpreact has std about 5 and 61% of tanh outputs sit beyond ±0.99
the loss reads only the output layer; the hidden layer's saturation needs a histogram of h

retrieve.q: Walk one minibatch through the BatchNorm MLP in training mode and then one example through it in eval mode. At each step, say which statistics are used, which tensors change, and which don't get gradients.
answer: training: hpreact = embcat @ W1 (no b1), then the column mean and std over the 32 rows, standardise, γ·x̂ + β, tanh, W2, loss
under no_grad, the running mean and std move 0.1% toward this batch's (momentum 0.001); they are buffers and get no gradient
backward fills grads for C, W1, W2, b2, γ, β only; the update moves those
eval: the same example uses the running buffers instead of batch stats, so its output no longer depends on batchmates and a batch of 1 works (p(correct) 0.0129 instead of nan)

retrieve.q: A colleague says: "We use BatchNorm, so init and learning rate don't matter any more." Using this course's measurements, say which half is right and which half is wrong.
answer: right about the forward pass: with BN the activation histograms are the same at gain 1 or 5/3 (std 0.63–0.65, about 2% saturated), and no fan_in scaling still gives healthy activations
wrong about the step size: BN divides the weight scale c out, so the gradient shrinks by c and ud moves by −2·log10 c
gain 0.2 raises ud by +1.40 (25× bigger steps); no fan_in scaling drops it to −3.74 … −4.19 and needs lr 1.0 to reach about −2.6 … −3
so the lr must be re-read from the update:data plot whenever the init changes; and BN brings its own costs (batch coupling, the eval-mode bug)

retrieve.q: Rank the three instruments in this course (the step-0 loss, per-layer histograms, the update:data ratio) by what each can and can't see, with one failure from the course that only that instrument catches.
answer: step-0 loss: one number, catches a confidently wrong output layer (27.8817 vs 3.2958), blind to the hidden layers
histograms of act and grad per layer: catch a wrong gain (0.5 → layer-5 std 0.02, 16× smaller gradient at layer 1) and saturation, but not the step size
update:data: catches a step size off by orders of magnitude (lr 0.001 → about −4.5; BN with gain 0.2 → +1.40) and an outlier layer (the last layer), blind to saturation
use all three: they are cheap (one forward and backward pass, or one line in the loop)

compare.q: z2h-4's big ideas judged the model from the outside: overfit one batch, pick lr from the loss, compare train and dev. This course looks inside. Which of z2h-4's checks would have passed on the starter net, and which of this course's instruments would have flagged it, and at what cost?
answer: z2h-4's net trained to dev 2.17 and looked fine by every loss-based check; its problems only cost 0.04–0.07 of dev loss on one hidden layer
the step-0 loss check flags the output layer at once (27.8817 vs 3.2958); a histogram of h flags the 61% saturation
z2h-4's lr finder reads one number for the whole net; the update:data ratio reads one per weight matrix and shows an outlier layer
the cost of looking inside is one forward and backward pass; the payoff grows with depth, where z2h-4's outside view can't say which layer is sick

compare.q: The big-ideas card states six claims; this overview gives one formula and a pipeline. Which claims does the BatchNorm formula already contain, and which ones only show up in the probes or the levers table?
answer: contained: standardise the preactivations (claim 4) and, through μ and σ coming from the batch, the coupling that forces test-time buffers (claim 5)
not contained: the step-0 loss check and the tanh gate (claims 1 and 2), which motivate the formula rather than appear in it
gain / √fan_in (claim 3) is the rule BN replaces for the forward pass, but not for the step size
looking inside (claim 6) lives in the probes and levers: the formula says what BN does, the probes say whether it worked

predict.q: The next course writes every backward pass by hand. Before seeing BN's: for each hidden unit, what should the gradient of the loss with respect to the pre-BN value, summed over the 32 examples of a batch, come out to? Which number in this course already told you?
predict.answer: Zero, up to float rounding. Adding the same constant to every row of a column raises the batch mean by exactly that constant, and BN subtracts it again, so the loss cannot change in that direction. The sum over the batch of that gradient is exactly what b1.grad would be, and the batchnorm-forward lab measured b1.grad at 4.4e-10. A hand-written BN backward that doesn't sum to zero per column is wrong: a free check for z2h-6.

apply.task: Do Karpathy's exercise E01 on the one-layer MLP from this course: set C, W1, b1, W2 and b2 all to zero, train 20,000 steps with the lecture's loop (batch 32, lr 0.1 then 0.01 after half), and print the step-0 loss, the largest |value| of each parameter afterwards, and the train and dev loss. Then explain, using the gate and the matmul backward, exactly which parameters trained and what the net learned.
apply.done: Step 0 prints 3.2958 (all logits 0, so uniform); after training C, W1, b1 and W2 are still exactly 0 and only b2 moved (max |b2| 2.59); train 2.8227 and dev 2.8211, which is the loss of predicting each character's overall frequency (the training set's entropy, 2.8226, from the step-0 loss card) and far above the fixed net's 2.1027.
apply.hint: h = tanh(0) = 0, so W2.grad = hᵀ·dlogits = 0; and the gradient into h is dlogits·W2ᵀ = 0, so nothing reaches W1, b1 or C. Only b2's gradient (the column sums of dlogits) is nonzero, so the net becomes a unigram model. Measured on the M3 in about 2 s.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: the zero-sum of BN's input gradient, or which instrument catches which failure?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why BN makes the activations gain-proof but not the update:data ratio, or why a bias before BN gets no gradient?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: weight scale → saturation → closed gates, or batch statistics → coupled examples → buffers and the eval flag?
If a new deep net won't train, which of the three probes would you run first, and which card would you reopen to read it?
Can you redraw the mental-model sketch from memory, including where b1 goes and what the dashed test-time box holds?
